doc.title: Ken Peplowski interviewed by Monk Rowe, Aspen, Colorado, October 10, 1997 [interview 1 of 2]

title: The jazz party audience and its future
summary: The knowledgeable, conservative, aging jazz party audience and its exclusivity.

story.theme_name: Where jazz stands today: young players, rock, and the audience
story.community_name: Is jazz healthy? Young players, rock and the future

blocks.x: Well that’s great to hear, I’m glad you brought all that up. At these jazz parties, the audience we see at them seems to be, I see a lot of the same people, and I guess they’re pretty knowledgeable about the music. It seems to be somewhat of a social event, but they seem to be pretty knowledgeable about the music.

They are pretty knowledgeable, yeah. They tend to be a little bit conservative in their musical taste but if you accept the job you have to kind of play within those parameters. They’re not going to want to hear even Thelonious — you know like “Ugly Beauty” or something, or an Ornette Coleman tune. Although once in a while if I get in a set with Howard, Howard Alden or somebody like that, a sympathetic ear or a sympathetic musician, we will throw something at them like that, and cover it up with a bunch of tunes that they know. And then they see maybe it’s not too far apart, these two different things. But yeah it’s an older, kind of conservative audience, but they are knowledgeable and they love this music and they’re very devoted obviously because these people fly around from one city to another. And it’s odd in fact, because you do see the same faces.

The first time we went to one I hadn’t even heard that these things existed and I was just, at first I was so impressed. I mean you could overhear people having conversations about this guy’s latest record and who was in the rhythm section and I’m looking at these people you know — this couple is 60 years old and they’re into this that much. And it’s great.
I don’t know how long it will last.

Well there’s less and less of these. Because it’s an older audience. Frankly they’re dying off. And it’s always been, they’ve been proud of the fact that it’s a closed circle of people.
